1.pericope_label: In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion

debates.q: Why has the psalm no title, and who wrote it?

sides.view: It had none because it was written as part of the preceding psalm, as many manuscripts show
David in the revolt of Absalom, adapting an earlier psalm of his own to a later affliction
Jeremiah — the anthological method and the slow, prosaic style are his

debates.q: What is asked for in the third verse?

sides.view: A rock of defence — many manuscripts read munition rather than habitation
A cliff, the word being distinct from the one used just before
A habitation, asked by a man driven out of his own house

outliers.view: Assign the psalm to Jeremiah on stylistic grounds alone, arguing from its borrowing method and its loose, sparingly adorned manner

4.pericope_label: Deliver me, O my God, out of the hand of the wicked; for thou art my hope

debates.q: In what sense is he a wonder to many?

sides.view: A portent or type — a typical person whose experiences refer to another
A monster, pointed at as something to be avoided or mocked
A shocking spectacle in his present distress, driven from his palace by his son

debates.q: What does the sixth verse say God did at birth?

sides.view: The received rendering is a doubtful expedient; read he that severed me, with the Greek corrected
He sustained a life that could not yet understand the power preserving it
He upheld being, life, food and raiment from the womb onward

outliers.view: Reads the psalmist calling himself a wonder as a claim to be a type, so that his own history is to be interpreted of another
Suggests the retrospect fits Israel personified as well as the individual, and notes the psalm has been treated as an epitome of the history of the Church

9.pericope_label: Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth

debates.q: Is the ninth verse a petition or a promise?

sides.view: A promise — thou wilt not cast me off, and as the outward man decays the inward is renewed
A petition, answered by the doctrine that God never casts off those he foreknew
A petition arising from fear that the Master may tire of the servant

debates.q: What does the taunt that God has forsaken him prove?

sides.view: Nothing — God never shows favour or displeasure by outward prosperity or adversity
That the godly may be forsaken for a small moment, but never finally
Only that enemies grow bold in weakness, as dogs howl over a dying lion

outliers.view: Denies flatly that worldly prosperity or adversity is any index of God’s pleasure, calling the contrary merely how men judge
Converts the closing imprecation into prediction — they shall be confounded, the words being prophetic denunciations

14.pericope_label: But I will hope continually, and will yet praise thee more and more

debates.q: What is meant by going in the strength of the Lord?

sides.view: Entering the tabernacle in the mightinesses of God
Coming into the temple carrying the tale of his mighty deeds
Three senses at once: not in his own strength, into the strengths of God, and into the house of God

debates.q: Is the plea of the eighteenth verse personal or national?

sides.view: It may be either — a parallel elsewhere shows the prayer can be the nation’s
Personal, and the grey hairs are added to make the plea more affecting
Personal, like a faithful old soldier receiving consideration from his king

outliers.view: Admits the psalmist adds grey hairs to old age because it was calculated to make a deeper impression, and defends the tactic as the reasoning God invites
Reads the verse on lifelong teaching as an argument for sacred conservatism against those who leave the gospel for the colleges of philosophy and scepticism

19.pericope_label: Thy righteousness also, O God, is very high, who hast done great things

debates.q: Is the twentieth verse singular or plural?

sides.view: The written text has quicken us — a sign the psalm was for congregational use
The divergence is noted and the Targum follows the plural, but the troubles are David’s own
Singular, and the quickening is the resurrection of one who was not to see corruption

debates.q: May Christians use the instruments of the twenty-second verse?

sides.view: No — with these, or anything like them, Christians have nothing to do in divine worship
Yes — the best music, vocal and instrumental alike, belongs to the best of masters
The verse says only that the singing accompanies the playing

outliers.view: Uses a verse of praise to exclude instrumental music from Christian worship altogether
Denies the Fathers’ reading of body and soul united in praise, then concedes the poet wished for exactly that
